\section{What carries the shortcut decides the fix}\label{sec:guide}\label{sec:solution}
The location law says what masking cannot do; it does not by itself say what to do instead. We evaluated the
mitigation families that a practitioner can apply to a frozen encoder, grouped by the supervision they need
(Table~\ref{m:tab:remedies}; full results, methods and ablations in Supplement~S8). Three regimes emerge, and the
linear-Gaussian account (Sec.~\ref{sec:theory}) explains each.

\input{tables/main_inroi_compact}

\paragraph{(1) Distinct overlays that carry the shortcut in their pixels} Sonographer calipers and synthetic rulers,
debris and tubes. Masking removes an out-of-ROI copy and leaves an in-ROI copy. Without any
artifact annotation, erasing from the frozen features the subspace along which \emph{generic} synthetic overlays move
the representation of masked images (mask-then-erase, U-MtE; Supplement~S8) removes most of what masking leaves:
thyroid $+0.222$ [$+0.197, +0.251$] over masking with DINOv2, $+0.204$ [$+0.174, +0.237$] with MedSigLIP and
$+0.128$ [$+0.112, +0.145$] with a ConvNeXt, and erasure beats augmentation with the same overlays (thyroid $+0.207$
[$+0.182, +0.235$]). With image-level artifact labels, group balancing on top of it is the most robust option
(Table~\ref{m:tab:remedies}).

\paragraph{(2) Artifacts that resemble the pathology} Capsule debris versus erosion fibrin. Any subspace estimated
from artifact appearance also contains disease evidence ($\rho$ large in Sec.~\ref{sec:theory}); unprotected erasure
is worse than masking ($-0.115$), protecting the label directions removes the failure but not the shortcut
($-0.010$ [$-0.020, -0.001$]). With image-level artifact labels masking plus last-layer retraining is the most robust
option (0.88).

\paragraph{(3) Shortcuts carried by correlates of the artifact} Dermoscopic hair co-varies with body site, age and
sex; a chest drain comes with a treated lung. Removing every hair patch with an oracle mask gains only $+0.015$;
no pixel- or insertion-based method closes the gap, and label-based reweighting (DFR, group balancing) is required.
The oracle-removal ceiling on a handful of annotated images diagnoses this regime.

\paragraph{Remedies do not transfer to unaltered test data} The regimes above are defined on the traps, whose reversed
test sets are extreme by construction. On the unaltered test distributions (Sec.~\ref{sec:natural}) no remedy is
uniformly better than the unmasked model: \input{tables/review2_guide_natural}.
We therefore offer the regimes as a decision guide for \emph{auditing} a model, not as a claim that any remedy
improves deployment performance:
(i) measure where artifacts sit relative to the ROI; out-of-ROI artifacts are what masking removes;
(ii) for in-ROI artifacts estimate which regime applies (oracle-removal ceiling, resemblance to the pathology);
(iii) evaluate any mitigation on shortcut-conflicting cases \emph{and} on the unaltered distribution, reporting clean,
correlated and reversed performance together, because a reversed-environment gain can be manufactured by removing
diagnosis signal (Supplement~S8).
